analysis.one_liner: Protects millions of acres of Northern Rockies federal land as wilderness, off-limits to new logging, mining, and drilling.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with 8 cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee without a hearing or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put millions of acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming into the National Wilderness Preservation System, plus wild and scenic rivers and wildlife corridors connecting big ecosystems like Yellowstone and Glacier. Once land is designated wilderness, road building, timber harvesting, mining, oil and gas drilling, and ski resort construction are banned there, and the land is managed for undeveloped recreation, clean water, and wildlife. The bill also sets up paid restoration work on damaged land and creates a system of biological corridors so wildlife can move between protected areas as the climate changes. It has been sitting in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee since March 2025 with no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who hunt, fish, hike, and camp on public land get permanent protection of the scenery, trails, and native fish and wildlife habitat they use. Downstream communities and farms benefit from protected headwaters that the bill says yield cleaner water and lower treatment and irrigation costs. Local businesses would get contracts for restoration work on damaged land, creating outdoor trades jobs. Taxpayers benefit from ending below-cost timber sales and other subsidized extraction that the bill says lose the Treasury money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hunters, anglers, hikers, and downstream water users

how_it_helps.text: It permanently protects millions of acres of federal land across Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming from road building, logging, mining, and drilling, keeping the land open for hunting, fishing, and backcountry recreation [S2].

The bill's findings say roadless land produces clean water for farming, ranching, and municipal supplies, and that protecting headwaters of the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, and other rivers would lower water treatment and irrigation costs [S2].
It would create restoration jobs by establishing rehabilitation zones on damaged federal land and awarding contracts to local businesses [S2].

It would stop below-cost timber sales and other subsidized extraction that the bill says costs taxpayers money, and would connect protected ecosystems with wildlife corridors so species like grizzly bears and salmon can move as the climate changes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies lose access to millions of acres of federal land they could otherwise log, mine, or drill. Ski resort developers are explicitly barred from building in designated areas. Motorized recreation users — snowmobilers and off-road vehicle riders — lose ground they currently use. Some rural logging communities would forgo timber jobs and the related county revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation bans motorized recreation — snowmobiles, off-road vehicles — and new development including ski resorts on the designated land, taking away access and business some local users and resort operators rely on today [S2].

Ending timber harvest on designated national forest land would reduce logging supply and cost logging jobs in rural communities — communities the bill itself describes as having high unemployment and dependence on resource extraction [S2].

None of the nine sponsors is from Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, or Wyoming — the five states whose land would be locked in — so the people most affected have no champion for the bill in the Senate [S2].
Designations are permanent; a future community or industry that wanted to use the land for something else could not easily reverse it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of the last large, intact wildland region south of Canada — clean water, wildlife habitat, and recreation that the bill's findings say is worth more left undeveloped than the timber and minerals would return to the Treasury [S2]. The costs are real: timber, mining, and oil and gas operators lose access to millions of acres, motorized recreation users lose ground they currently ride, and some rural communities would forgo logging work the bill itself says those communities depend on [S2]. The bill tries to offset the job loss with funded restoration and corridor work, but restoration jobs are temporary and scattered, while timber losses are permanent for the designated areas [S2]. On balance, the design is straightforward — it does what wilderness bills do — and its main weakness is political, not structural: no senator from an affected state supports it [S2].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has not scheduled a hearing or vote on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 27, 2025 [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — appears in the record after that referral [S4].
Eight senators signed on as cosponsors: seven Democrats and one Independent [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the timber, mining, and oil and gas interests that could develop the land, and motorized recreation users, keep the status quo — the land remains open to the uses the bill would have banned. The general public gains nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests, so far

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to referral in the Senate [S2].

against.name: Mike Lee
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Chairs the committee the bill was referred to on March 27, 2025; no hearing or markup has been scheduled and no action appears in the record since referral [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors are Democrats or the Independent from Vermont; no Republican and no senator from the five states affected has signed on, and the committee that controls the bill is chaired by a Republican [S2, S3].

industries.note: Timber harvesting is expressly defined as 'development' and would be banned on all designated wilderness, corridor, and recovery land — the largest single withdrawal of federal timber the bill would cause [S2]. The bill frames this as ending below-cost sales that lose taxpayers money [S2]. Its interest runs against conservation of the land for public recreation and water quality.
Mining is named as a banned 'development' across the designated areas, closing millions of acres of federal land to new claims and extraction [S2].
Oil and gas drilling is defined as 'development' and prohibited on the designated land, removing acreage from future leasing and exploration [S2].

industries.industry: Ski resort developers and motorized recreation
industries.note: Ski resort construction is expressly listed as banned 'development', and wilderness status bars snowmobiles and off-road vehicles from areas some currently use [S2].
Existing grazing generally continues under wilderness law, but the bill lets permit holders voluntarily donate their permits for retirement, gradually shrinking grazing on the protected land [S2].

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation, outfitting, and restoration contractors
industries.note: Protected scenery and fisheries support hunting, fishing, and wilderness-based recreation, and the bill creates funded rehabilitation zones and contracts for local businesses doing restoration work [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The Congress runs through January 2027, so the bill is technically alive, but the realistic path is what has happened to this same bill in prior Congresses: it has been reintroduced repeatedly for decades and has never gotten a committee vote or a floor vote. With 9 sponsors, no support from the five affected states, and a Republican chair deciding whether the Energy and Natural Resources Committee takes it up, the likely outcome is that it sits without a hearing until the Congress ends.
